title: Linear regression: noise and held-out evidence
subtitle: Fit a straight line using training observations, then inspect residuals and test error.
objectives: Interpret the fitted slope, intercept, and signed residuals.
Relate noise to scatter while recognizing finite-sample variability.
Distinguish training fit from evidence on held-out test observations.
assumptions: One dimensionless predictor x spans 0–10; y = 2x + 1 + σz, with independent standard-normal z.
Ordinary least squares includes an intercept and uses only the randomly assigned training rows (75%, rounded down).
Controls use σ from 0–5, 20–300 rows, and an integer seed from 0–4294967295. Initial settings are σ=1, n=100, seed=42.

Changing noise with the same seed and sample count preserves normal draws and split. Because the generating truth is exactly linear, residuals scale with σ and train/test MSE scale with σ², apart from floating-point roundoff. Changing the sample count may change the realization.

MSE is the mean squared residual, in squared response units. Comparisons across different random realizations, seeds, or splits need not be monotonic in noise. Training and test errors have no guaranteed ordering.

questions.question: A point lies above the fitted line. What is the sign of its residual?
questions.answer: Positive: residual = observed y − predicted y, so an observation above the line exceeds its prediction.

questions.question: What should happen when σ is zero, provided training x varies?
questions.answer: The fit recovers slope 2 and intercept 1, with train and test MSE near zero within floating-point tolerance. All observations lie on the true generating line.

questions.question: Does a smaller training error alone prove better performance on new data?
questions.answer: No. Training error describes the observations used for fitting. Test observations remain outside the fit and supply held-out evidence. In a finite sample, test error can be smaller or larger than training error.
